0.title: Character Creation
0.content: . | Roll Ability Scores: Roll 3d6 for each, in order: Strength, Intelligence, Wisdom, Dexterity, Constitution, and Charisma. | Choose a Kindred: Select a Kindred. Note that Elves, Grimalkins, and Woodgrues cannot be Clerics or Friars, as they have no spiritual connection to the deities of mortals. | Choose a Class: Select a Class. | Adjust Ability Scores: If you wish, you may raise your Prime Abilities, corresponding to the class you picked, by lowering other ability scores. For every 2 points by which a score is lowered, 1 point may be added to a prime ability. No ability may be lowered below 9 or raised above 13 by this method. | Note Ability Modifiers: Now your character’s ability scores have been determined, make a note of any associated bonuses or penalties. |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |   | . | Ability Score | 3 | 4-5 | 6-8 | 9-12 | 13-15 | 16-17 | 18 | . | Modifier | -3 | -2 | -1 | 0 | +1 | +2 | +3 | . | Note Kindred and Class Traits: Record any special traits possessed by your character as a result of their Kindred and Class, including Attack Bonuses, Save Targets, Skill Targets, and Languages Spoken. | Roll Hit Points: Determine your character’s Hit Points by rolling the die for the chosen Class and adding your Constitution Modifier. | Roll Equipment: All Characters start play with Common Clothes, a Backpack (containing 2 Preserved Rations, a Waterskin, and a Tinder Box), and a Belt containing 3d6 gold pieces. In addition, certain Classes may have additional weapons, armor, and special items. Finally, you may choose or roll up to 4 items from the Adventuring Items table, and roll for an odd, slightly magical trinket corresponding to your character’s Kindred. | Note Armor Class: Your character’s armor class (AC) is determined by the armor they wear, and their Dexterity modifier. Some Kindreds and Classes also grant a bonus to AC. | Note Speed: Your character’s speed is based on the amount of equipment carried. | Choose Alignment: Determine your character’s Alignment. Clerics and Friars may not be Chaotic. | Note Level and XP: Your character begins play at Level 1 with 0 XP. | Name and Details: Choose a name for your character. Your may use the tables listed under your character’s Kindred for inspiration. Optionally, select or roll for a background and any extra details associated with your character’s Kindred. | . You are now ready for adventure! .

1.title: Classes
1.content: . | Classes . | Bards | Cleric | Enchanter | Fighter | Friar | Hunter | Knight | Magician | Thief | . | .

2.title: Bards
2.content: Musicians and poets drawn to a life of wandering and adventure. Their Prime Abilities are Charisma and Dexterity. Their Hit Die is a d6. As they level, they become better at Listening. They also have three additional Bardic skills: Decipher Documents allows them to get the gist of non-magical texts in a language they do not speak, Legerdemain allows them to perform sleight of hand tricks, and Monster Lore allows them to identify monsters and their basic powers and vulnerabilities based on their appearances in Myth and Folklore. Once per turn, Bards can play music to Counter Charm, giving allies immunity to magical effects based on music and song, and +2 to Saving Throws against Fairy Magic. Once per day per level, Bards may Enchant creatures to Fascinate them, causing them to devote utter attention to the bards song, and follow them while the Bard plays their song.

3.title: Cleric
3.content: Holy warriors in the service of the Pluritine Church. Their Prime Ability is Wisdom. Their Hit Die is a d6. They must be Lawful or Neutral in Alignment, and follow the Tenets of their Holy Order or fall from grace. They may Detect Holy Magic Items by touch and concentration, cast Holy Magic at higher levels channeled through a Holy Symbol, and Turn Undead once per Turn, attempting to drive off the Undead through the might of the One True God.

4.title: Enchanter
4.content: Wanderers who wield Fairy Magic. Their Prime Abilities are Charisma and Intelligence. Their Hit Die is a d6. Enchanters have an additional Skill, Detect Magic, which enables them to detect subtle resonances woven into an enchanted object via touch. They are granted the use of Fairy Runes, the secret sigils of the Fairy Rulers, as well as a minor magical talents known as a Glamours. However, by allying themselves with the godless world of Fairy, they are Resistant to Divine Aid.

5.title: Fighter
5.content: Mercenaries, Soldiers, and Ruffians, experienced in combat and warfare. Their Prime Abilities are Strength. Their Hit Die is a d8. They possess Combat Talents which grant them exceptional abilities in melee and ranged combat.

6.title: Friar
6.content: Wandering Ascetics spreading the Gospel of the Pluritine Church. They are only loosely affiliated with The Church and exist outside the strict religious hierarchy of the Clergy, thus beloved by the common folk, whom they often aid when The Church does not. Their Prime Abilities are Intelligence and Wisdom. They have a Hit Die of d4. They must be Lawful or Neutral in Alignment. A Divine Blessing gives them an Armour of Faith, giving them a bonus to AC. They have a Skill target of 5 for Survival when Foraging. They are efficient in the use of Medicinal Herbs, can cast holy Magic, and can Turn Undead once per Turn. However, they have taken a monastic vow of Poverty, and must donate excess wealth to worthy causes (not other PCs), and dress in a simple habit and cut their hair in tonsure.

7.title: Hunter
7.content: Expert trackers, stalkers, and killers, at home in the wild woods. Their Prime Ability is Constitution and Dexterity, and they have a Hit Die of d8. A Hunter may forge a bond with an Animal Companion. Hunters have three additional skills: Alertness, which prevents them from being Surprised, Stalking, which allows them to remain undetected in the light brush of the wilds, and Tracking, which allows a Hunter to find tracks and follow them. They gain a +1 Attack Bonus to Missile Attacks, and may take Trophies from creatures they have hunted and use them as lucky charms. They are Wayfinders that are less likely to find their way when lost.

8.title: Knight
8.content: Warriors who serve a noble, doing their bidding and upholding their honor. They serve a Liege, one of the eight Lower Houses of The Dolmenwood. Their Prime Abilities are Charisma and Strength, and have a Hit Die of d8. They are expert Horseman, easily assessing steeds and gaining a +1 Bonus to Attack while Mounted. They are Monster Slayers, gaining a +2 Bonus to Attack against Large creatures. They have Strength of Will, gaining a +2 Bonus to Saving Throws against fear-based effects.

9.title: Magician
9.content: Connoisseurs of secret arcane lore. They hone innate sparks of magical sensitivity through years of arduous study, imprinting patterns of magical energy into their mind (a process known as memorizing a spell) to be unleashed at a later date. Their Prime Ability is Intelligence, and they have a Hit Die of d4. A Magician starts with a single Spellbook which gives them three Arcane Spells, but may only cast one a day. They have an additional skill, Detect Magic, which enables them to detect subtle resonances woven into an enchanted object, place, or creature, through touch.

10.title: Thief
10.content: Rogues who live by skills of deception and stealth. Their Prime Ability is Dexterity and their Hit Die is a d4. Thieves are proficient in Backstabbing, dealing deadly blows when attacking from behind with a dagger. They have five additional Skills: Climb Wall allows them to climb vertical sheer surfaces with only minimal handholds without specialized equipment, Decipher Document allows them to get the gist of non-magical texts in a language they do not speak, Disarm Mechanism allows them to disarm complex, clockwork-like traps and mechanisms using Thieves Tools, Legerdemain allows them to perform sleight of hand tricks, Pick Lock allows them to open a lock without a key using Thieves Tools, and Stealth allows them to make a Stealth Check to remain undetected when shadows are the only cover.

12.title: The Basic Game Procedure
12.content: . | The Referee Describes the situation, depicting the environment, characters, hazards, and objects present, and noting any smells, sounds, or other features. | The players ask Questions to clarify description elements. | The players put themselves in their characters shoes, discussing what to do, and then Declaring Actions they wish to perform. This can be anything imaginable, from speaking to characters present, interacting with the environment, or using a special capability granted to them by their Kindred or Class. The Referee clarifies potential risk involved with such actions. Each Character may perform a different action, though it usually beneficial for a Party to stick together and act in concert with one another. | The Referee Judges the potential results of the proposed action. Specific game rules may apply, and an appropriate Resolution System may apply, or the Referee will come up with a ruling based on the specific situation. The Referee presents the odds to a player, making the likelihood of success and failure and potential risks clear. The player may then alter their approach, or come up with alternate plans to tip the odds in their favor. | The action is Resolved, potentially involving some kind of dice roll. Then Time Passes, depending on the action taken. Time is normally divided into discrete segments called Rounds (10 Seconds) and Turns (10 minutes). In hazardous environments, a Wandering Monster roll may be made to determine if the Party encounters something by chance. | .

14.title: Skill Checks
14.content: Some actions require passing a Skill Check to succeed. All adventurers can use the Listen, Search, and Survival skills. Some classes grant the use of additional, specialized skills. To make a Skill Check, roll a d6, and add any situational modifiers. If the roll equals or exceeds the character’s Skill Target, they succeed in the Skill Check, and the action they carry out succeeds. A natural 1 always fails and a natural 6 always succeeds.

15.title: Ability Checks
15.content: An Ability Check represents a test of a character’s physical or mental aptitudes (one of their Ability Scores) rather than a particular learned skill. Roll a d6 and add the Ability Modifier of the relevant Ability. If the result equals or exceeds a target number of 4, the check succeeds. A natural 1 always fails and a natural 6 always succeeds.

16.title: Saving Throws
16.content: Certain dangerous or detrimental effects call for a Saving Throw, or Save, which is a roll to determine whether a character avoids the effect. There are 5 Save Categories, each for a different type of hazard. Roll a d20 and add applicable modifiers. If the result equals or exceeds the character’s Save Target for the relevant Save Category, the Saving Throw Succeeds. Doom are effects that instantly kill or inflict ongoing physical malignancies, such as poison, disease, and death magic. Ray are effects coming from rapidly moving, directional effects, such as lightning bolts. Hold are effects that hinder or prevent movement, such as paralysis or falling rocks that may crush or pin characters. Blast are effects that fill a wide area, such as explosions. Spell applies to potent, directly targeted effects, such as arcane or holy spells. In situation not covered by the rules, the Referee should run down the categories listed above, choosing the first that fits the effect in question. If an effect does not fit in any category, default to Doom.

17.title: Attack Rolls
17.content: This roll is used to determine whether an attacker lands a blow on an opponent. Roll a d20 and add any applicable modifiers (your Attack bonus, as well as your Strength Modifier for Melee Attacks, and Dexterity Modifier for Ranged Attacks). If you beat or exceed the defender’s Armor Class, you succeed.

18.title: Luck Check
18.content: Used when the outcome of a situation depends on pure chance. The Referee proposes a chance of success, and a relevant dice is rolled to determine if the Luck Check succeeds.

19.title: Example Resolutions
19.content: . | If players wish to make a reasonable climb (e.g. climbing a tree) in a non-pressured situation, no Check may be required. In more difficult or tense situations, a Dexterity Ability Check may be required to succeed, with a Failure resulting in the Character falling halfway through making the climb. | A stuck door that is unlocked but so obstructed that it cannot be opened without force may be shoulder barged with a successful Strength Ability Check. The Referee should probably warn the player if this will produce a loud noise, which may attract attention to the Party. Similarly, a Locked door may be broken open with an axe or crowbar with a successful Strength Ability Check. Alternatively a Locked Door may be picked by a thief using a Pick Lock Skill Check, or open via a magic spell (likely with no Check required). | When two groups approach one another, there is a chance one or the other will be unaware of the other’s presence. This is handled with a Surprise Roll, which is a Luck Check for each group, with odds depending on the vigilence of the other party. | .

20.title: Encounter Procedures
20.content: Encounter Procedures apply when adventurers meet strangers, foes, or monsters in the wild. | The Referee determines the Awareness of each party of one another. This applies if a group is making a lot of noise, or carrying a light in the dark. | The Referee rolls for Surprise, if one party is not aware of the other. The standard chance of being surprised is 2-6, but may be modified in certain situations. | The Referee determines the Distance between the two groups when encountered. | The Referee determines the Initiative, i.e. which side acts first. Each side rolls a d6, the highest roll determining whom goes first. | Both Sides declare their intended Actions. If one side decides to start attacking the other side, begin following Combat Procedures. If one side wishes to avoid the encounter, it may attempt to Flee the encounter. A side may attempt to Parley with the other, and provided combat has not been initiated, a Charisma bonus may determine a Monster or NPC Reaction to the party. | .

21.title: Combat Procedures
21.content: . | Both sides declare their Intended Actions. The intention to cast a spell must be declared, because the spell is disrupted if the caster loses initiative and is harmed. The intention to flee from melee must be declared, for opponents that win initiative against a fleeing combatant are able to attack their opponents with a bonus. | Each side rolls d6 to determine Initiative, who acts first. | Each side, in order, moves and attacks. Combatants may not move while casting spells. | The Referee makes a Morale Check for NPCs, if applicable. | .

22.title: Alternate Alignment System
22.content: Law and Chaos are diametrical cosmic forces in the universe. The tension between Law and Chaos give rise to the very threads from which gods, fairy, mortals, and reality itself is woven. Law is frequently associated with ‘Goodness’, Chaos with ‘Evil’, but these are generalizations, not rules. Neither are truly benevolent or malevolent. All beings have an Alignment which represents a character’s orientation on the cosmic scale, the ratios of the cosmic threads from which a person’s soul is woven. In practice, there are infinite ways by which a being’s soul may be tied to the universe, as many ways as there are styles to braid the cosmic threads together. But for the purposes of game mechanics, beings are categorized under one of three alignments: Law, Neutrality, or Chaos. Alignments have nothing to do with a character’s allegiances, personality, or morality; whether or not a character with either of these alignments is actively engaged in the Cosmic Struggle, their souls are marked with a cosmic affiliation nonetheless. Animals and other creatures of lesser sentience tend to be neutral, but not always. Characters of Neutral Alignment are also embodiments of Law and Chaos, but these exist in a more balanced state within the character’s being than those of Lawful or Chaotic alignment. Neutrality is not a cosmic force in the universe. Player characters are free to select whichever Alignment they choose, though Clerics must be Lawful, and Friars cannot be Chaotic. GM’s should not use Alignment as a tool to police the behavior of aligned characters. But there are powerful beings and institutions within The Dolmenwood with the ability to do so, as they entwine fates, drawing aligned characters to their banner’s cause. Because Alignments represent fundamental forces of the universe, a character’s Alignment may predicate very real mechanical effects and consequences as they interact with the magic, monsters, and more powerful beings within The Dolmenwood.

23.title: Law
23.content: Law is the force of order, stability, and harmony, but also stagnation, imprisonment, and fascism. The Cosmic Struggle of Law is to ensure the events of the world inevitably march on their flawless, unchanging plans towards the ultimate, irrefutable truth of the universe. As time moves on, all distraction and resistance to this plan will falter, until everything will be in its perfect state forevermore, without alteration or the possibility of possibilities. Those who are Lawful in Alignment are part of this inevitable destiny, awash on the turbulent seas of fate, but often have little knowledge of what that destiny is and what their role will be in fulfilling it. So those that pursue the Cosmic Struggle of Law are forever looking for signs and omens to show them their proper way.

24.title: Chaos
24.content: Chaos is the force of change and freedom, but also destruction, indifference, and lawlessness. Chaos is the howling maelstrom beyond the veil of shadows and existence. It bends and tears the fabric of the universe; it destroys all that seeks to be permanent. It allows great miracles as reality alters at the whim of those that can call upon the eldritch forces, and it causes great catastrophe as beings we call demons (and far, far worse) rip into our reality and lay waste to all. Everything that is made will be unmade. Nothing exists, and nothing can ever exist, not in a way that the cosmos can ever recognize. Those who pursue the Cosmic Struggle of Chaos consider the world in terms of ebbing and flowing energy, of eternal tides washing away the sand castles that great kings and mighty gods build for themselves. To be Chaotically Aligned is to be an attractor to higher beings and cosmic forces in need of pawns in the pursuit of needless goals. Many who are aligned with Chaos desperately wish they were not.

25.title: Neutrality
25.content: To be Neutral is merely to exist between the forces of Law and Chaos. Most beings in the universe are born with Neutral Alignment, and remain so unless drastic measures (often unwittingly followed) realign the cosmic threads of their existence. In the real world, every human being that has ever existed has had Neutral Alignment; Law and Chaos are fantastical supernatural forces unlike any of us have experienced in our mundane lives. Examples of the most Lawfully Aligned characters are those deeply bound with the concept of fate, whether they are fulfilling a predetermined destiny or attempting to escape it. Such figures include Luke Skywalker, King Arthur, Paul Atreides, Buffy the Vampire Slayer, or The Antichrist. The most Chaotically Aligned characters are granted supernatural powers to change the world as they will it, or characters which always seem to run into destruction or misfortune. Examples of Chaotic characters include Superman, most wizards, and almost all of The Muppets.

27.title: Home
27.content: Dolmenwood? Well, let me tell ye, everything you ever heard about the Wood is true and everything you ever heard is false. Dreams and fairies walk between standing stones and dancing trees, slipping in and out of the mortal world as easily as you or I slip through an open door. It’s right pretty though. Dare I say, beautiful even. All manner of enchantment lingers beneath its boughs. It’ll capture your heart if ye let it. And that sounds as lovely as a song until you realise the Wood’ll never, ever give it back without paying the proper cost.” . Dolmenwood is a game about exploring the beguiling realm of Dolmenwood - a swathe swathe of tangled woods, fungus-encrusted glades, and foetid marsh on the wild borders of civilisation: . | Explore the wild places of the Wood, travelling through bramble-choked dells, fungal forests, and accursed bogland, bedding down among root and bracken amid the nocturnal babbling of strange beasts. | Unearth treasure hoards in forgotten fairy ruins, haunted manors, dripping caverns, crystal grottoes, unhallowed barrow mounds, and abandoned delvings. | Confront fell beasts, roving fungal monstrosities, terrible wyrms, tricksome fairies, and restless spirits of the long deceased. | Recover saintly relics and shrines lost in the befuddling tangle of the Wood, gaining the favour of the Church by returning them to civilisation. | Forage for weird fungi and herbs in the untrod depths of the woods, many with useful magical powers — and many that can be sold for profit. | Strike against Chaos, defending civilisation from the encroaching forces of the wicked, half-unicorn Nag-Lord who lurks in the corrupted northern woods. | Unravel secrets of deep magic, charting the obelisks, dolmens, and ley lines littered throughout Dolmenwood — but beware the sinister Drune cult that wards them. | Seek the counsel of witches or the sinister Hag, wielders of magic that can heal, hex, or divine the future. Meddle in the affairs of nobility, allying with a noble house in its intrigues and power plays in the courts of High-Hankle and Castle Brackenwold. | Journey along fairy roads, ancient magical paths bordering on the ageless world of Fairy that allow travel throughout Dolmenwood — and perchance to realms beyond. | Return to the homely hearth to share tales of peril with quaint locals over a mug of ale and a well-stoked pipe. | .

28.title: Kindred
28.content: . | Kindred . | Mortals . | Human | Breggle | Mosslings | . | Fairies . | Elves | Grimalkin | . | Demi-Fey . | Woodgrue | . | . | . Kindred are sentient folk divided into three types: Mortal, Fairy, or Demi-Fey. There are six playable options.

29.title: Mortals
29.content: Kindred from the mortal world. They suffer from Mortality, with a lifespan counted in decades, and suffer from all manner of diseases and ailments. All but a select few mortals have No Innate Magic, and most are mistrustful of magic, viewing it as perilous and unnatural. Most mortals are Religious, worshiping deities, exalted heroes, ancestors, and spirits, and those who dedicate themselves to the service of a religion may receive blessings in the form of holy spells. They cluster together in large towns in The Dolmenwood for safety. Human . As is the way in the wider world beyond The Forest, Humans are found throughout The Dolmenwood. Most humans are adherents to the Pluritine Church, the dominant religion in Dolmenwood, and the official religion of the Duchy of Brackenwold. The Church worships a nameless, male god, referred to as The One True God. Daily practice focuses on venerating Saints, exalted people who performed miraculous deeds on behalf of the Church, now said to be intermediaries between Mortals and God. They believe naming or depicting God is heresy, that sentient life is sacred and must be protected and nurtured, that free will is fundamental yet evil deeds must be punished (in life and through eternal damnation in hell), and that God created the world of Fairy to demonstrate the folly of life without faith and salvation. The old religions worshiping the Old Gods of The Wood have mostly been swept away, yet remnants of the worship of the old gods live on in folklore and tradition. For instance, many humans believe consuming mead and ale is a means of communion with greater powers, hearkening back to the worship of The Green Man, god of feast, ale, revelry, and hunting. Rumors say the witches of Dolmenwood still worship the Old Gods in secret. Human adventurers are commonly found among all Classes. Yet rare is the human with enough connection to Fairy to become an Enchanter. Mechanically, Humans tend to be more Decisive than other Kindred (humans act first on a tied initiative roll), exhibit Leadership more naturally than others (the loyalty rating of Retainers is increased by 1), and are Quick To Learn (+10% to XP Earned). Breggle . A proud, thick-furred, stubborn Folk, sometimes called Goatfolk (or Hregl in their own tongue). Once the sole masters of the fertile hills and meadows of the High Wold in the Southwest Dolmenwood, the ancient Breggle noble houses rule alongside humans, swearing fealty to the Dukes of Brackenwold. Breggles often live alongside humans, in towns and hamlets and cities, sometimes intermarrying. In human towns, Breggle are treated with respect and caution, as the power of the Longhorn noble houses is known and feared. They saw that the horns of a Breggle grow as they earn wealth and renown, and the length of a Breggles horn indicates their social class: the shorthorns form the working class, and the longhorns the noble class. Theoretically, a wealthy shorthorn’s horns may grow to the size of a longhorn, but acceptance in the ruling class is another matter. As subjects of Duke Brackenwold, Breggles are nominally adherents to the Pluritine Church. True devotion is rare, however, as Breggles tend to offer up prayers to esteemed ancestors from their long history, a practice they call Aud frengd Hlerr, roughly translating to ‘Praising the Ancestors’. Aud frengd Hlerr teaches that the worlds of Mortal and Fairy are but testing grounds, and those that honor their families gather in an afterlife of eternal feasting, whereas those that lead craven and spiritless lives enter a dismal realm of torment, where there souls are annihilated by gnawing worms. Breggle adventurers are most commonly fighters, knights, or magicians. They seldom seek membership of the Pluritine Church as clerics or friars, and only very rare individuals have enough connection with Fairy to become Enchanters. Mechanically, Breggle are Furry (+1 AC when unarmored or wearing light armor), and have Horns (which they can use to make attacks with). Longhorns may use their Intense Gaze to force humans and Shorthorns into submission. Mosslings . Mosslings are a gnarled and woody Shortfolk native to Dolmenwood, gathering in small, isolated communities in the dark, dank forests of The Dolmenwood, burrowing their homes into the damp earth or inhabiting natural caves. They are stocky, pudgy, with green, yellow, or brown skin, textured like wrinkled bark and patched with mold. Mosslings become wiser and more plant-like as they age. After death, even their bones rot away to mold. Their body decays to a rich compost within a year. Mossling adventurers are commonly Fighters or Hunters. They are only occasionally accepted into the ranks of Dolmenwood nobility as Knights, seldom seek membership in the Pluritine Church as Clerics or Friars, and rarely possess enough connection with Fairy to become Enchanters. Mechanically, Mosslings have a Skill Target of 5 for Survival when Foraging, and are Resilient, having a +4 Bonus to Saving Throws against fungal spores or poisons, and a +2 bonus to all other Saving Throws. As a Mossling ages, their dank, fertile flesh picks up seeds and spores germinating into Symbiotic Flesh, which gives them a new trait at each level. Mosslings also know a carefully guarded, quasi-magical craft called a knack.

30.title: Fairies
30.content: Kindred from the realm of Fairy. Fairies are Immortal; they do not age, suffer from non-magical disease, or die naturally, though they may be killed. They are Innately Magical, natives of a world where mortal logic holds no sway. Unless disguised, Fairies are Unearthly; animals are invariably unnerved, and most Mortals will have never met a fairy, and perceive them with awe, fear, and caution. Fairies are Non-Religious; Fairies have no gods, and have no spiritual connection to mortal gods. Instead Fairy societies have myriad cosmologies and philosophies of living. Fairies are wracked with passions deeper than Mortals can fathom. They can be at once wise with measure and petty as children, with an unwavering devotion to their personal whims. As the basest of all metals, the rarefied bodies of Fairies are burned by the touch of Cold Iron (Pure Iron), and suffer additional damage when hit by weapons made from such weapons. The touch of silver is repulsive to Fairies, instantly bringing on a queasiness of the stomach. They are Highly Resistant to Magic, gaining a +2 Magic Resistance. Most Fairies never venture into the mortal world, but the more romantic, obsessive, or adventurous may gain a taste for the place. Fairy PCs have chosen to come to the mortal world, and Players should consider their reason for departure when creating Fairy characters (for example, in exile, fleeing some peril, or simply wishing for a new start). Elves . As humans dominate the Mortal World, Elves do so in Fairy, forging vast kingdoms, subjugating others under their rule, and delving deeply into the secrets of magic. Elves are physically similar to humans but vary widely in apperance, with features such as pointed ears, small horns, or star shaped pupils. It is always possible to identify an elf for they carry an air of unearthliness about them (unless disguised by magic). Many kinds of elves in the boundless reaches of Fairy: the Pale-Elves of The Lightless Realms, the dark skinned, the Crystal-Rimed Elves of The Cloud Palaces, and the cold-hearted Frost-Elves who serve the wicked Prince of Winter, among countless others. Elves enjoy being addressed by curious epithets hinting at their True Names in the tongue of Fairy (which they never reveal to Mortals). Elves who frequent Dolmenwood sometimes take on a nickname (a shortened version of their epithet) or a Mortal name, for convenience. Elves who wander into the Mortal World may be fascinated with Mortal Kindred, with their short, spirited lifespans and inevitable aging and death. Some elves view Mortal company as peculiar and entertaining, while others earnestly seek to comprehend the Mortal mindset. Elves tend to be on good terms with other Demi-Fey and Fairies. Elves are commonly Enchanters, Fighters, Hunters, or Magicians. It is rare for an Elf to be accepted into the Dolmenwood nobility as a Knight. Elves cannot be Clerics or Fighters as they have no spiritual connection with Mortal Gods. Mechanically, Elves have a Skill Target of 5 for Listen and Search. They possess a minor magical talent known as a Glamour. They possess an Unearthly Beauty which gives them +2 to Charisma when interacting with Mortals. Grimalkin . Shape-shifting, Cat-Fairies renowned for their Illusion Magic and love of eating rats. They originate in the Fairy realm of Catland, ruled by the fearsome Queen Abyssinia, the Queen of All Cats. Normally, Grimalkin take Estray Form, appearing as a humanoid cat, wearing clothing, speaking, and walking upright. In Chester Form, a Grimalkin resembles a normal cat in all aspects, though perhaps a little fatter; they can understand language, but only respond in yowls and meows. In Wilder Form, a Grimalkin is difficult to perceive, appearing only as a gleaming pair of deranged, predatory eyes. In this form they are at their most Primal and Fey, indiscriminately attacking friend and foe. Grimalkins who wander in the Mortal World tend to become jealous and furtive among their own kind, so tend to prefer the company of other Kindred. They mostly regard the earnest undertakings of Mortals as comical and absurd. They are greeted with curiosity and wonder in human settlements, perhaps due to Human’s affection for domestic cats. Grimalkin are commonly bards, enchanters, hunters, or thieves. It is rare for a Grimalkin to be accepted into the ranks of Dolmenwood Nobility to become a Knight. Grimalkin cannot be Clerics or Friars as they have no spiritual connection with Mortal Gods. Mechanically, Grimalkin are Small, and must wear armor tailored to their small size, and cannot wield Large weapons, but gain a +2 to AC in melee with large creatures. They can Hunt Rats to gain HP. They possess a minor magical talent known as a Glamour. They have a Skill Target of 5 for Listen. They can spend a round to Shapeshift into Chester Form freely, and into Wilder Form once per day.

31.title: Demi-Fey
31.content: Kindred with origin in the realm of Fairy that have taken up permanent residence in the mortal world. Over generations, exposure to the mortal world has changed the Demi-Fey. They are Mortal, but with a lifespan of centuries. They have Remnants of Magic, diminished by long exposure to the mortal world. Demi-Fey are Superstitious. They have no spiritual connection to mortal Gods, instead accumulating odd beliefs and lore since arriving in the mortal world and derived from esteemed fairy ancestors. Demi-Fey retain their ancestor’s vulnerability to Cold Iron, but have grown accustomed to silver. Woodgrue . Woodgrues are capricious, bat-faced goblins who, many generations ago, forsook their ancestral home in Fairy and migrated to the dells of the Mortal World. They have massive, flapping ears and soft, downy fur upon their heads and chests, while the rest of their body appears like that of a human child. Woodgrues live a nomadic lifestyle, wandering Dolmenwood alone or in small groups, following where their whims and nose lead. They love wild dancing and cacophonous music. The magic of Fairy lingers in the music of Woodgrues, for their songs can enchant folk to frolic into the deep woods. Woodgrues delight in using this magic for mischief and high jinks. While mischievous and rascally, Woodgrues only cause serious harm if slighted. In human settlements, Woodgrues may be met with caution, as folks are aware of their rambunctious nature. However, it is known that barring Woodgrues entry would likely only lead to greater misfortune. Woodgrue adventurers are commonly bards, magicians, or thieves. It is rare for a Woodgrue to be accepted into the ranks of the Dolmenwood nobility as a knight. Woodgrues cannot be clerics or friars as they have no spiritual connection with the deities of mortals. Mechanically, Woodgrues are Small, and must wear armor tailored to their small size, and cannot wield Large weapons, but gain a +2 to AC in melee with large creatures. They are Compelled to Jubilate; if witnessing a celebration they are utterly compelled with every fiber of their being to partake (they may resist with a Save Versus Spell, but feel drained and downtrodden for the length of the engagement). Once per day, a Woodgrue may play an enchanted Mad Revelry on a wind instrument while hooting and dancing terribly, with various results. A Woodgrue can see in the darkness up to 60’, viewing the world as if glowing with a faint moonlight (fine detail cannot be perceived). And Woodgrues have a Skill Target of 5 for Listen.
